sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in LLMs have demonstrated strong generalization ability across wide range of real-world applications. In parallel with these developments, one line of work adapts LLMs to downstream tasks through training-based methods such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023), and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024), which update the model parameters to align with task-specific objectives. However, these training-based methods often demand large amounts of preference data (Ouyang et al., 2022) or hundreds of thousands of rollouts (Shao et al., 2024). The inefficiency of these methods motivated complementary line of work that seeks to adapt LLMs in training-free manner by engineering the prompt or context of LLMs rather than altering their intrinsic capabilities. Early efforts in this direction mainly rely on human heuristics to engineer the instructions (Agrawal et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2025a; Khattab et al., 2024; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) that elicit LLM reasoning capabilities (Wang et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023a) or execute better workflow (Hu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Shinn et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025a; Yao et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2025). In-Context Learning (ICL) (Brown et al., 2020) enables few-shot learning via in-context examples. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and its variants (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023a) instruct LLMs to generate intermediate reasoning steps. Later, agent frameworks (Yao et al., 2023b) rely on the reasoning to take actions, allowing LLMs to interact with external tools and environments. However, such methods are designed to accomplish tasks in single attempt but cannot learn from accumulated human trials recorded in offline datasets. For example, CoT may avoid mistake in one attempt through reasoning, but the same error may recur in subsequent trials. 1 CoSTA@NUS Preprint Figure 1: Overview of our work. We investigate whether LCEs can engineer effective context and further examine the mechanisms underlying their successes and failures. Given set of training examples, LLM as Context Engineer (LCE), or automatic context engineering, was proposed to learn context from data without parameter training (Cai et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). The main principle is to cast the LLM itself as context engineer that operates on textual space rather than parameter space (Yang et al., 2024). Multi-prompt Instruction Proposal Optimizer v2 (MIPROv2) (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024) and Genetic-Pareto (GEPA) (Agrawal et al., 2026) propose effective sampling strategies for searching over candidate prompts. Training-Free Group Relative Policy Optimization (TF-GRPO) (Cai et al., 2025a) extracts semantic advantages by comparing agent rollouts, while Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) (Zhang et al., 2026) curates an evolving context and uses metadata to track the contributions of each insight. Despite their success, these methods are typically evaluated using different LLMs and distinct benchmarks, leaving their relative advantages and broader applicability unclear. For example, ACE (Zhang et al., 2026) reports improvements with DeepSeek-V3.1-671B (DeepSeek-AI, 2024) on agentic (Trivedi et al., 2024) and financial tasks (Loukas et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025), whereas GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) reports improvements with Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025) and GPT-4.1-mini (OpenAI, 2025) on math (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and multi-hop reasoning (Yang et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020). These inconsistencies in evaluation protocols motivate us to conduct comprehensive benchmark of LCEs across LLM families and diverse tasks under comparable evaluation settings. As summarized in Fig. 1, our major contributions in this paper are as follows. (1) We conduct comprehensive comparison between LCE methods in unified benchmark, using various LLMs, LCE methods, and task types. (2) We also evaluate the effect of scaling model parameter size and model generations. (3) We conduct new ablation studies and case studies to show when and how LCEs can actually work. Our key findings are as follows: LLMs can engineer contexts via task-specific training, but no single method can achieve the best performance in all datasets at test time. Scaling helps but cannot reverse existing failures of LCEs. Even scaling to newer generations and more parameters remains insufficient to make LCEs more effective across different settings. When&How: Through aggregate analysis, we find that LCEs work better when facing less diverse failure modes of reasoning. Case studies show that the ability to abstract principled contexts from heterogeneous failures is the major bottleneck and that the success of some LCE methods is attributed to the improvement in adherence to (format) instruction rather than reasoning.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: AI Agents. AI Agent frameworks can be viewed as test-time scaling methods that allocate additional inference-time computation to organize the operation of LLMs during task execution, without modifying 2 CoSTA@NUS Preprint the model parameters. CoT prompting (Wei et al., 2022) is widely adopted starting point for eliciting the reasoning capabilities of LLMs by generating intermediate steps before the final answer, achieving substantial improvements across diverse downstream applications. Building on CoT, self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) samples multiple reasoning chains from the same prompt and selects the final answer by majority voting to improve reasoning reliability. Beyond purely internal reasoning, ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b) interleaves reasoning traces with task-specific actions such as tool calls, allowing the model to ground its reasoning in external observations rather than relying solely on parametric knowledge. Another research line extends reasoning into more structured trajectories. Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023a) frames reasoning as search over tree of intermediate thoughts, allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths. Graph-ofThoughts (Besta et al., 2024) further extends this paradigm by representing intermediate thoughts as nodes in reasoning graph, enabling more flexible aggregation, recombination, and refinement of partial solutions. Despite this progress, these frameworks rely on predefined workflows and offer limited flexibility in adapting to specific tasks. Our study therefore focuses on analyzing methods that automatically engineer contexts in training-free manner. LLM Context Engineers (LCEs). Similar to training-based methods, LCEs follow the same optimization loop but rely on textual feedback and updates to the context text rather than gradient-based parameter modifications. Automatic Prompt Engineer (Zhou et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026) pioneers this paradigm by searching over LLM-generated instruction candidates to maximize task accuracy. Optimization by Prompting (Yang et al., 2024) casts the LLM itself as an iterative optimizer that refines prompts based on past trajectory. Deep Language Networks (Sordoni et al., 2023) extend this idea to stacked LLMs by jointly optimizing prompts via variational inference. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) introduces self-reflection feedback loop where the model verbally reflects on task outcomes and conditions subsequent attempts on these self-generated critiques. Building on these advancements, subsequent methods move beyond instance-specific reflection toward optimizing reusable system prompt that encodes general strategy for the target task. DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) provides unified toolkit inspired by PyTorch abstractions for declaratively programming LLM pipelines. Within this framework, MIPROv2 (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024) and GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) propose different sampling strategies to optimize the instructions. Inspired by backpropagation in neural networks, TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) uses natural language to propagate textual gradients. Recently, another line of work maintains an evolving external context, such as abstract experiences or reusable skills (Cai et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). TF-GRPO (Cai et al., 2025a) and ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026) contrast successful and failed task executions to extract reusable insights. ACE (Zhang et al., 2026) curates an evolving playbook through iterative bullet-level updates. Despite the success in the reported benchmarks, the inconsistent evaluation makes the actual effectiveness of LCEs unclear. Thus, this work aims to uncover and understand the limitations of LCEs.

We include diverse tasks: mathematical reasoning (MATH500, Lightman et al. (2024)), multi-Hop reasoning (HotpotQA, Yang et al. (2018)), instructions following (IFBench, Pyatkin et al. (2025)), retrieval (MiddleMatch, Leviathan et al. (2025)) and Agentic Tasks (AppWorld, Trivedi et al. (2024)). Each experiment is repeated 5 times with 5 fixed seeds. The validation set was used to select engineered context during training. Our results show that TF-GRPO, GEPA, and ACE consistently improve validation performance across the four datasets. On MiddleMatch and IFBench, all LCEs improve validation performance, with maximum gains exceeding 20 points for ACE on IFBench and 10 points for GEPA. On MATH500 and HotpotQA, TF-GRPO, GEPA, and ACE achieve only marginal validation gains, while TextGrad fails to produce effective contexts and even leads to substantial performance decline of more than 15 points on HotpotQA. No free lunch for LCEs at test time. Beyond validation, we compare these methods at test time, where we only use three methods (TF-GRPO, GEPA, ACE) that stably improve validation performance. To evaluate LCEs in multi-step agentic settings, we additionally include AppWorld, benchmark requiring LLMs to complete long-horizon tasks to further assess whether LCEs remain effective when task completion requires sustained interaction rather than single response. We include three LLM families in our evaluation: Qwen3-8B (Qwen3), Gemma-4-E4B-it (Gemma4) (Gemma Team, 2026), and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2512BF16 (Min3) (Liu et al., 2026). Table 2 reports the performance on different datasets across three LLM families and the performance changes relative to each LCEs initial, with CoT and ICL included as reference baselines. (1) LCEs provide limited advantages over simple baselines. Although these LCEs can improve validation performance, these gains do not consistently transfer to the test set, where LCEs can even underperform simple baselines, or the gains cannot be attributed to the algorithm itself. To assess LCEs effectiveness on the test set, we first examine the absolute performance differences between the best-performing LCE and the best baseline, reported in the best column of Table 2, and find that only 7 of the 15 settings show observable improvements (best > 1). We further examine these gains using statistical significance tests, which indicate that only 5 settings show significant improvements (p < 0.05). Even among these settings, we observe that some gains stem from the initial context design rather than from engineering better context during training, 5 CoSTA@NUS Preprint Figure 3: Ablation on the scale of the Reflector and Generator across four datasets. Scaling the reflector cannot rescue failures but further enhances existing improvements. through comparisons between the final and initial performance of the best-performing LCEs. For example, GEPA on IFBench with Gemma4 surpasses CoT by 6.94 points but remains 1.22 points below its initial performance. Meanwhile, we notice there are some wins of LCEs over CoT or ICL for specific models on HotpotQA and MATH500. But the wins occur only when models baseline performance is lower than that of other models on the same task. For example, on HotpotQA, Min3 has the lowest CoT and ICL scores among the three models (23.07 and 27.07, respectively), while ACE raises its score by 3.13 compared to its initial. Yet, LCEs yield no performance gains for the other LLMs. Thus, we conjecture that such gains are more likely when the models capabilities are not fully exploited. (2) No clear winner among LCEs across datasets or models. For example, TF-GRPO performs best on AppWorld with Qwen3, while ACE leads on Min3. We also observe that LCEs substantially improve Gemma4 on MATH500 but provide limited performance gains for Qwen3 and Min3. On HotpotQA, LCEs improve Min3 more than the other models. The limitation suggests that there is no free lunch for LCEs different models/datasets may need different LCE algorithms. The limited generalizability of LCE methods encourages us to further investigate the working mechanism in the later sections. LCE with Scaling. After testing LCE methods with 8B-scale models, we further investigate whether scaling up models can improve the effectiveness of LCEs. (1) Bigger Reflector Can Cause More Gain but Also More Loss. In Fig. 3, we investigate whether larger LLMs can engineer better context for smaller models or vice versa. We define the Reflector as the model that generates reflections to engineer the context, and the Generator as the model that executes tasks using the optimized context. Then, we conduct experiments on four datasets using GEPA, TF-GRPO, and ACE, varying the sizes of the Reflector and Generator between 8B and 32B. We observe that although larger LLMs engineer more effective context in most settings on IFBench and MiddleMatch, they can even perform worse than smaller models on MATH500 and HotpotQA. (2) Bigger/Newer Models Do Not Necessarily Enable LCE Better Than Smaller/Older Ones. In addition to scaling the reflector and generator separately, we jointly scale the self-reflecting model from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-235B-A22B across four datasets (Qwen Team, 2025). Fig. 4 shows that model scaling primarily strengthens the underlying task solver, while the effectiveness of LCEs remain inconsistent. On MiddleMatch, both GEPA and TF-GRPO outperform CoT across model sizes, with particularly large gains at 235B. On IFBench, both methods match CoT at the 235B scale but fail to engineer useful context at smaller scales. In contrast, neither method yields reliable gains on MATH500 or HotpotQA: improvements at some smaller scales disappear or even reverse as the model grows. Thus, more parameters are insufficient to make LCEs consistently effective. We further investigate whether newer LLM generations lead to better LCE behavior. As shown in Fig. 4, although baseline performance generally improves across generations, the gains from LCEs still exhibit no consistent trend. For example, GEPA shows smaller gains on HotpotQA as the LLM generation advances, while it continues to show substantial gains on MiddleMatch. Overall, these results provide no clear evidence that newer LLM generations systematically lead to better LCE behavior.

sections.title: 5 When & How Can LLMs Engineer Effective Context?
sections.content: In addition to the aggregated Table 2, we will conduct qualitative and quantitative analysis to uncover the failure/success mechanisms of the LCEs. When Do LCEs Work? In Table 2, which method is effective is not simple. We notice the largest gain (best LCE versus best baseline) in MiddleMatch, and the smallest gain in MATH500. In Ministral, LCEs are more useful than in Qwen3. Thus, we suppose both the data and the model play roles here. The intuition is that the LCEs learn from the models failed rollouts and therefore the rollouts hinge not just on data but also on models. Specifically, we hypothesize that LCEs are more effective when rollouts exhibit homogeneous failure modes. To examine this hypothesis, we analyze the correlation between failure-mode diversity in the initial rollouts and performance gains across all experimental settings (model, dataset, methods). We characterize failure-mode diversity through the following steps: (1) Embedding Rollout Failure-modes. For each failed reasoning rollout, we diagnose its cause by using an LLM. We instruct an LLM to summarize the cause mode, grounded in specific evidence and expressed in generalizable terms without instance-specific details (see exact prompt at Fig. 14). We then encode each failure mode as vector using the embedding model all-mpnet-base-v2 (Song et al., 2020). The embedding model is widely used for short text; for example, ACE uses it to detect duplicate items in the playbook. (2) Measuring Diversity. We randomly subsample extracted failure-mode text samples and use the Vendi Score (Friedman & Dieng, 2023) to quantify failure-mode diversity. This score has been used to quantify pattern diversity, such as the diversity of generated images (Stein et al., 2023). The score ranges from 1 to and can be interpreted as the effective number of distinct samples. The lower scores indicate more homogeneous failure modes. Detailed experimental setup is in Section B.2. In Fig. 5, we present the performance gains versus Vendi scores and the mean/standard deviations of them on the axes. Performance gain is defined as the performance score difference between after and before LCE. We can see that different datasets present different diversity and the variance comes from models and LCE initial prompts. MiddleMatch is the least diverse task, and AppWorld is the most diverse given that its task is to handle interactions with an app. 7 CoSTA@NUS Preprint Our major findings are: Figure 5: Left: Correlation between LCE performance gains and the Vendi Score of failure modes. Markers and error bars show means and standard deviations on both axes for LCEs. The significant negative correlation indicates that LCEs tend to achieve larger performance gains when failure modes are less diverse. Right: Changes in the Vendi Score of experiences across epochs. The small changes imply that LCEs struggle to distill experiences into shared principles. (1) Less Diverse Failure Modes, Better The LCEs Work. The left figure clearly shows the negative correlation between diversity and performance gains across all LCE methods. GEPA and TF-GRPO present the statistical significance, but ACE does not. We conjecture that differences in context updates may explain this pattern. GEPA rewrites prompts, while TFGRPO modifies or merges selected experiences. These updates may lose useful knowledge when failure modes are diverse. ACEs incremental accumulation may better preserve such knowledge, making its performance gains less dependent on failure-mode diversity. To further control for the potential influence of other factors, we conduct mixed-effects analysis in Section G. The negative association between failure-mode diversity and performance gains remains significant, which is consistent with the above observations. (2) In contrast, the ICL gains turn out to be irrelevant to the diversity. That means the relation hinges on the LLM operations, for example, reflection on failures, which are missing from ICL. (3) In Fig. 5 (Right), we show how the Vendi Score of experiences (e.g., distilled insights or bulleted playbook) extracted by ACE and TF-GRPO from training rollouts changes over epochs across different models and datasets. The Vendi Score changes very mildly across iterations. That means the LLMs are not able to reduce the diversity of experiences by iteratively optimizing context, which explains why LCEs do not perform well on highly diverse tasks. (4) Beyond the above findings, we also conduct further analyses of potential factors influencing LCE effectiveness in Section H. Factors, like optimization budgets across LCEs and differences in baseline task accuracy, do not show significant correlations with the performance gains. Failure-mode Diversity Mainly Comes from Data. To identify the main sources of variation in failure-mode diversity across settings, we decompose the variance of Vendi Scores into dataset, model, and LCE main effects, together with residual variance. In Fig. 6, we show the variance decomposition proportions. larger variance proportion for factor indicates greater differences in failure-mode diversity across its categories. The calculation step of the variance decomposition is provided in Appendix B.3. In the figure, the small variance proportion attributed to the model suggests that failuremode diversity varies relatively little across models, whereas the large proportion attributed to the dataset indicates substantial variation across datasets. This suggests that failure-mode diversity is driven primarily by the dataset, with some datasets naturally eliciting broader range of failure modes. For example, the high similarity in MiddleMatch queries contributes to its low failure diversity: In MiddleMatch, questions are generated using fixed template: Heres list of names: nn{sequence of names}nn What is the single name that appears right between <name_1> and <name_2>? Such homogeneous data patterns make the reflection complexity lower and therefore lower failure mode diversity. How Do LCEs Work? We have seen that LCEs work well on low-diversity datasets but it also happens, though not frequently, that LCEs can sometimes improve performance on high-diversity tasks. For example, in MATH500 with Gemma4 and HotpotQA with Min3, LCEs exhibit high variance in both performance gains and failure-mode Vendi Scores ( Fig. 5). Here, we conduct case studies to understand how LCEs conquer Figure 6: Ratio of total variance in Vendi Score of failure modes. 8 CoSTA@NUS Preprint Table 3: Performance under different experience utilization and retrieval settings. Figure 7: LCE behavior on HotpotQA. Top: Example of verbose prediction from Min3 leading to failure. Bottom: LCEs reduce the false failure rate in Ministral alongside performance gains. Figure 8: LCE behavior on MATH500. Top: Example of format failure from Gemma4. Bottom: LCEs improve compliance with the required format in Gemma4 while improving performance. Case Study: LCEs improve adherence to the task instructions. In multiple samples, we notice that the experiences extracted in LCEs are related to the output format or instruction details, less relevant to problem solution ideas. (1) In HotpotQA, by investigating the generated samples, we find that Min3 tends to generate verbose answers for problems, which sometimes cannot be identified as an answer by the evaluation. One example is given in Fig. 7 (Top), where we show that both answers contained the correct answer (bolded) but LCE makes the model produce the recognizable answer. For HotpotQA, the evaluation relies on exact matching of answers, and thus only the LCE answer is considered correct. Beyond the example, we found that the improvement of LCEs on HotpotQA is related to the reduction of such False Failure. During optimization, LCEs repeatedly identify this verbosity failure and reinforce conciseness through instructions such as Answer only what the question asks. Avoid extraneous details. Concretely, in Fig. 7 (Bottom), we show that the accuracy increase is related to the reduced False Failure rate, i.e., the proportion of predictions marked as incorrect by Exact Match that, however, actually contain the ground-truth answer. (2) For MATH500, we observe that Gemma4 frequently fails to follow the format requirement, such as Put the final answer in boxed{...}, as illustrated in Fig. 8 (Top). Thus, in Fig. 8 (Bottom), we report format compliance before and after optimization across models. We found that LCEs reinforce this instruction in the optimized context, improving format adherence and contributing to Gemma4s performance gains greatly. Details on calculating the false failure rate and format compliance are in Section B.4. Moreover, we apply an LLM-based answer extractor to standardize final-answer extraction in Section and find that the performance gains of LCEs decrease substantially after extraction, further suggesting that the improvements of LCEs 9 CoSTA@NUS Preprint come from the better instruction adherence. Case Study: TF-GRPO. To further investigate method-level failures, we conduct an additional ablation study with TF-GRPO, whose framework follows the general principles in Eq. (1) with clearly separated workflow stages and achieves the best performance in more settings in Table 2 across LCEs. In Table 3, we compare the ablations under two representative performance regimes based on whether LCE beats baselines: ICL > LCE > CoT and LCE CoT > ICL. Here, we add two inference variants that use fixed number of experiences or in-context examples: (1) GRPO-ICL RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) retrieves in-context demonstrations used during TF-GRPO training, excluding query samples that can be solved in all rollouts. (2) All-Exps Random randomly samples experiences from all experiences produced by TF-GRPO (Final-Exps). The RAG variants retrieve items based on semantic similarity to the retrieval query using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025c), which supports encoding long in-context demonstrations. Beyond the inference variants considered above, we also evaluate several additional variants. As these experiments offer limited new insights, we report the full results in Section E. Experience extraction (E) plays the most critical role. Across all four cases, either catastrophic performance loss (left two columns) or gain (right two columns) starts from the All-Exps Random, where Experience Extraction was first introduced to the ablation. That means when LLMs did not extract useful experiences from rollouts, the performance will not be improved over simply ICL of rollouts. Instead, when useful experiences are extracted (i.e., gains via E), the shorter experiences improve performance. We conjecture it is due to the smaller context length. The conjecture can be supported by our observation in Section F, that lengthy contexts can diminish the benefits of useful knowledge in ICL.

sections.title: B Experimental Setup
sections.content: B.1 Experimental details for Benchmark and Scaling Experiments We use Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025), Gemma-4-E4B-it (Gemma Team, 2026), and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct2512-BF16 (Liu et al., 2026) for the main benchmark. Our scaling experiments examine both model size, from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-235B-A22B, and model generation, from Qwen1.5-7B to Qwen3.5-9B. For each task, we use the same configuration across all models and LCEs in both the main benchmark and the scaling experiments. For single-step experiments, we set the maximum output length to 16,384 tokens and the sampling temperature to = 0.7. For AppWorld, we use the same sampling temperature and maximum output length of 4,096 tokens per step. Methods. We adopt the official codebase of each method in our single-step experiment. GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) is officially supported in the DSPy package (Khattab et al., 2024), and we set auto="heavy" to maximize performance. For TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025), we use the official package with 3 epochs and batch size of 5. For TF-GRPO (Cai et al., 2025a), we follow the official setting with 3 epochs and group size of 5, using the original prompt templates for the critic and summarizer; to align with other methods and maximize performance, we run validation after each epoch and select the best experience pool. For ACE (Zhang et al., 2026), we use the official implementation with curator frequency of 5 and 3 epochs with bullet de-duplication. For AppWorld, we use the ACE and GEPA implementations provided in the official ACE codebase and adapt TF-GRPO to the same framework with the original prompts. We set the length limits for per-step execution outputs and the total message history to 10,000 and 200,000 characters, respectively. For ACE on AppWorld, we use the default settings: curator frequency of 1 and maximum of 5 Reflector refinement rounds. Each method is run with 5 random seeds ({0, 1, 2, 3, 4}). All models are served with vLLM on NVIDIA GPUs. Benchmarks and Datasets. In Table 4, we show that existing methods are mostly evaluated on disjoint datasets. To understand the landscape, we select variety of datasets with different reasoning patterns: Reasoning to find the solution (MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018)); Retrieval from long context (HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), MiddleMatch (Leviathan et al., 2025)); Following Instructions with unseen constraints (IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025)) and Agentic Tasks requiring multi-step planning and execution (AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024)). In these tasks, training-based methods like RLHF/RLVF have been shown to significantly improve LLMs capabilities (Ouyang et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017; Rafailov et al., 2023). But little work was done to examine the LCEs in these tasks in unified setting. MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024) is 500-problem subset of competition-level mathematics drawn from the MATH benchmark (Hendrycks et al., 2021). Following prior settings, we use 100/200/200 split for training/validation/test, and adopt Qwen-Verify to grade the results. HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) is multi-hop question-answering dataset in which the model must aggregate evidence across multiple documents. To unify the training framework across methods, we follow prior settings (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) and provide the gold and distractor passages directly in the context, thereby removing the retrieval stage. Following GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), we use 150/300/300 split and adopt exact match as the evaluation metric. IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025) is an instruction-following dataset designed to evaluate whether LLMs can comply with user instructions rather than merely answer the underlying question. Following GEPA (Agrawal 16 CoSTA@NUS Preprint et al., 2026), we use 150/300/294 split and adopt the official IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025) metric. MiddleMatch (Leviathan et al., 2025) is basic retrieval benchmark in which the model must identify the target name positioned between two given anchor names. We generate the data following the procedure of prior work, and use 100/100/300 split with exact match as the evaluation metric. AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) is benchmark of stateful tasks spanning multiple applications, where agents interpret user requests and interact with applications through APIs. sections.content: Good Context Boosts Smaller Model to Match Larger Ones. On MiddleMatch, we observe more consistent trend than other benchmarks: (1) Both methods with 32B Reflector boost the performance of the 8B LLM, and GEPA even pushes the 8B LLM (42.33 60.40) to match the 32B CoT baseline (60.67), though with larger variance (12.93 on 8B vs. 3.32 on 32B). (2) Both methods with an 8B Reflector enhance the 32B LLM compared to their own initial prompts, while only TF-GRPO with an 8B Reflector outperforms the best CoT baseline. Smaller Model can unlock the capability of Larger Model. On IFBench, GEPA generally benefits from scaling up the reflector  (Fig. 3)  , whereas TF-GRPO under the 32B generator slightly underperforms. Remarkably, while the 8B and 32B models show similar CoT performance (32.35 vs. 33.47), using an 8B reflector alone is sufficient to unlock the 32B models potential: GEPA pushes the 32B model to 39.08.

sections.title: E Case Study on TFGRPO with more variants
sections.content: We add two inference variants that use fixed number of experiences or in-context examples: (1) All-Exps RAG retrieves experiences from the full set of extractor-proposed experiences accumulated during TF-GRPO training. (2) Final-Exps RAG retrieves experiences from the final experience pool produced by TF-GRPO (Final-Exps). The full results are shown in Table 5. Which Is Better Context: More High-Quality Experiences Or Fewer Experiences? In-Context Demonstrations Can Mislead LLMs Into Making Errors. In settings where LCE CoT > ICL, replacing random demonstrations with retrieved training demonstrations reduces accuracy sharply from 68.10% to 26.50%. Our analysis identifies two main causes: (1) lengthy context impairs reasoning, and (2) demonstrations can distract models from the target problem. Training demonstrations are selected from problems with both successful and failed attempts. These problems are challenging for the model and may require more extensive reasoning to distinguish correct solutions from plausible alternatives, making GRPO-ICL demonstrations substantially longer than ICL demonstrations. To examine the effect of context length, we reduce the number of retrieved demonstrations to match the total context length of ICL, as shown in Table 6. This restores accuracy to approximately 68.10%, suggesting that excessive context length may contribute to the performance degradation, potentially by making it harder for the model to focus on critical reasoning steps. Meanwhile, we observe cases where Min3 answers demonstration question instead of the target problem. Thus, we report the ratio of responses that answer an in-context demonstration rather than the target problem. As shown in Table 7, we find that Min3 is difficult to distinguish demonstrations from CoSTA@NUS Preprint the target problem, leading to these failures. LCEs may mitigate this issue by extracting knowledge from demonstrations, leaving only target question to answer in the context. The above results suggest that lengthy contexts may be harmful, which is consistent with previous work. For example, Zhang et al. (2025b) observed that performance improves with few-shot ICL setup but declines with many-shot ICL, while Hong et al. (2025) showed that lengthy contexts can introduce noisy information and consequently hurt performance. However, another possible explanation for the failures is that GRPO-ICL demonstrations are of lower quality. To separate the effects of context length and quality, we conduct an additional controlled study using ICL. Since directly evaluating the quality of an evolving prompt is difficult and inherently subjective, we therefore construct MATH-Sync by paraphrasing each MATH500 question conditioned on its ground-truth reasoning trace. We validate correctness via majority voting and remove duplicates (cosine similarity > 0.9 or identical final answers), yielding 318 (synthetic, original) pairs. For each test problem, we use its paired synthetic paraphrase as gold ICL demonstration, which shares the underlying solution process with the test problem by construction and thus provides controlled high-quality context. We compare three baselines: (i) the original CoT prompt with no demonstrations, (ii) ICL with irrelevant demonstrations sampled from unrelated problems, and (iii) gold ICL using the matched synthetic paraphrase. As shown in Fig. 18, gold ICL substantially outperforms both other baselines, confirming that high-quality demonstrations are genuinely valuable when they are concise. We observe that the coefficient of failure-model diversity is significantly negative, implying that the LCEs can improve the context better when facing less heterogeneous failure modes. In the early regime, both padding strategies further improve performance, consistent with the intuition that more demonstrations help. However, as the prompt continues to grow, both curves eventually fall below all three baselines, including the original CoT prompt with no demonstrations at all. Crucially, this degradation occurs even under the repeated-gold setting, where every additional token comes from high-quality, perfectly aligned demonstration. Length alone is therefore sufficient to drive performance below baseline. Together with the gold ICL result, this shows that the value of an injected experience is not monotonic in either quality or quantity: high-quality information improves performance up to point, after which length-induced degradation overwhelms the benefit. Mixed-effects Analysis on Failure-mode Diversity To further control for the potential influence of other factors, including dataset identity, model identity, LCE methods, and initial performance, we use linear mixed-effects model to test our hypothesis that LCEs can achieve larger performance gains when failure modes are less diverse. Specifically, performance gain is defined as the outcome variable, incorporating failure-mode diversity, dataset identity, and initial performance as fixed effects, while treating models and LCE methods as random effects. We report the β and corresponding p-value from the t-test. As shown in Table 8, the coefficient of failure-mode diversity remains significantly negative (β = 0.05), which is consistent with our finding that LCEs can be more effective when addressing more homogeneous failure modes. Moreover, the coefficient for initial performance and the individual coefficients for the four datasets relative to AppWorld are not significant. Specifically, we quantify the optimization budget using two metrics: the number of LLM calls during optimization and the corresponding token consumption, including both input and output tokens. To assess whether different optimization budgets are associated with differences in LCE effectiveness, we conduct correlation analyses using the Qwen3 results across four datasets.
